title: Kubernetes Services, DNS and Ingress: Quick Revision
summary: Revision notes on how Kubernetes exposes and finds workloads. They cover labels and selectors, ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer Services, in-cluster DNS, and Ingress with ingress controllers.

chapters.title: Labels, Selectors and Endpoints
points: A Service is a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods. Pod IPs change whenever a Pod is replaced, so clients use the Service instead.
Labels are key/value tags on objects. A Service's spec.selector matches Pod labels with equality only (app: web), and all keys must match (AND).

The control plane turns matching Ready Pods into EndpointSlices, and kube-proxy programs those backends into iptables or IPVS rules. A Pod that fails its readiness probe is removed from the endpoints.
Comparison: a Service selector is equality-only map matching. Deployment, ReplicaSet and Job selectors also support set-based matchExpressions (In, NotIn, Exists).
Example: Pod labels app=web,tier=fe and a Service selector app: web match. `kubectl get pods -l app=web` and `kubectl get endpoints web` verify it.

Mistake: a selector typo or a Service with no selector gives empty endpoints, and traffic gets connection refused or timeouts. Also, port is the Service port, targetPort is the container port, and mixing them up breaks traffic.
Interview Point: (1) How does a Service find its Pods? (2) Why does a Service have no endpoints? (3) What is the difference between port and targetPort?

chapters.title: ClusterIP Service
points: ClusterIP is the default Service type. It gets a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster, so it suits internal service-to-service traffic.
The ClusterIP is virtual and not bound to any interface. kube-proxy rules DNAT traffic sent to it onto a random ready backend Pod, which gives basic load balancing.
Comparison: ClusterIP is internal only, NodePort adds a port on every node, and LoadBalancer adds an external cloud load balancer. Each type builds on the one before it.
Example: `kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080`, or a YAML Service with type: ClusterIP, port: 80 and targetPort: 8080.

Mistake: you cannot ping a ClusterIP, because it is virtual and only the Service ports respond. Test with curl or wget from a Pod instead. clusterIP: None makes a headless Service that returns the Pod IPs directly and is used with StatefulSets.
Interview Point: (1) What is a ClusterIP and who implements it? (2) What is a headless Service and when do you use one? (3) Why does ping to a ClusterIP fail?

chapters.title: NodePort and LoadBalancer
points: NodePort opens the same port on every node, from the 30000-32767 range by default. Traffic to <nodeIP>:<nodePort> is forwarded to the Service and then to a Pod.
LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to create an external load balancer, with a public IP or DNS name. It also creates a NodePort and a ClusterIP behind it.

Comparison: NodePort needs you to manage node IPs and firewalls, and is fine for dev or bare metal. LoadBalancer gives one stable external address per Service, but each Service creates its own cloud LB with its own cost.
Example: `type: NodePort` with `nodePort: 30080` pinned, or `type: LoadBalancer`. Then `kubectl get svc` shows EXTERNAL-IP as <pending> until the cloud provides one.

Mistake: EXTERNAL-IP stuck on <pending> on minikube, kind or bare metal means there is no cloud controller (use MetalLB or `minikube tunnel`). externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client source IP, but nodes with no local Pod then drop traffic.
Interview Point: (1) What is the NodePort range? (2) How do the three Service types relate? (3) Why use Ingress rather than a LoadBalancer per Service?

chapters.title: Cluster DNS
points: CoreDNS runs in kube-system and gives every Service a DNS name: <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Headless Services resolve to the Pod IPs.
Each Pod's /etc/resolv.conf has the cluster DNS IP, a search path (<ns>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local) and ndots:5. Short names are therefore expanded through the search path.
Comparison: `web` works only inside the same namespace. `web.prod` works across namespaces. The full FQDN `web.prod.svc.cluster.local` is the safest form.
Example: `kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup web.prod`. Also, StatefulSet Pods get stable names like pod-0.headless-svc.

Mistake: using a bare Service name for a Service in another namespace fails. DNS problems are usually CoreDNS Pods down or a NetworkPolicy blocking port 53. Check `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns`.
Interview Point: (1) What is the full DNS name of a Service? (2) How does a Pod resolve a short name like `web`? (3) How do you debug DNS failure in a cluster?

chapters.title: Ingress and Ingress Controllers
points: Ingress is an API object with HTTP/HTTPS routing rules by host and path, sending traffic to Services. It gives L7 routing, TLS termination and one entry point for many Services.

An Ingress object does nothing alone. An ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy, cloud ALB) watches Ingress objects and configures the actual proxy. The controller itself is exposed through a LoadBalancer or NodePort.
Comparison: a LoadBalancer Service is L4, one Service per LB, and has no host or path routing. Ingress is L7 with many Services behind one LB. Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor.
Example: rules with host: app.example.com, path: /api and pathType: Prefix routing to the api Service, plus ingressClassName: nginx and a tls: secretName for HTTPS.
Mistake: an Ingress with no controller installed, or with the wrong or missing ingressClassName, is silently ignored. A backend Service name or port typo gives 503 or 404 responses.
Interview Point: (1) What is the difference between an Ingress and an ingress controller? (2) Why use Ingress rather than a LoadBalancer Service? (3) How is TLS configured on an Ingress?

chapters.title: Services and Ingress Cheat Sheet
points: Types: ClusterIP is internal only (the default). NodePort exposes <node>:30000-32767. LoadBalancer is a cloud LB on top of the NodePort. ExternalName is a DNS CNAME. clusterIP: None is headless.
Selector flow: spec.selector matches Pod labels, giving EndpointSlices of Ready Pods. Debug with `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`, `kubectl get pods -l k=v` and `kubectl describe svc <svc>`.
DNS names: <svc> in the same namespace, <svc>.<ns> across namespaces, and <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local as the FQDN. CoreDNS lives in kube-system.
Ingress: needs a controller plus an Ingress with host, path, pathType, ingressClassName and a tls secret. It gives L7 routing behind a single LB.

Debug order for 'can't reach it': check the Pod is Ready, then the Service endpoints, then the targetPort, then DNS resolution with nslookup, then the Ingress class and controller logs. Interview Point: (1) Walk through a request from a browser to a Pod. (2) NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs Ingress? (3) Why are the endpoints empty?
